script.opening: (Jovial, big laugh, yawns once during the call.) "Doc, my wife's threatening to sleep in the spare room — my snoring's that bad. She also reckons I stop breathing and gasp, but I think she exaggerates. I'm a bit knackered in the day, sure, but who isn't. Can you just give me something for the snoring — a spray or strips or something? I just want a decent night's sleep."

facts.text: "She says I go quiet, then gasp and snort like I'm choking. She's been nudging me." Loud snoring for years, worse over 2 years. Gets up to pass urine twice a night. "I wake up feeling like I haven't slept." Morning headaches some days.

If asked when he dozes: "TV, definitely. Reading, yes. Traffic… sometimes." Epworth answers if the doctor goes through them: reading 2, TV 3, sitting in a public place 2, passenger for an hour 3, lying down in the afternoon 3, talking 0, after lunch 2, stopped in traffic 1 — total 16.

Only if asked directly about driving: "(pause) Once, recently. I caught myself drifting. Scared me, to be honest" — on the motorway last week, drifted onto the rumble strip. Drives HGVs 50 hours a week, often nights.
"A drink in the evening now and then. No tablets" — 2–3 pints most evenings to unwind.

"Not that I know. Collar size — I'd have to check" (it's 18 inches). BMI 34 at last check. BP was "a bit high" at a DVLA medical last year; not on treatment. No diabetes known. No regular medicines. No allergies. Smokes 10 a day.
Married to Sunita, two teenage children, mortgage. Self-employed HGV driver for a haulage firm.
"Honestly? The job. If this is something, am I going to lose my licence? I've got bills."

Cheerful and minimising; laughs off the gasping. Gives the near-miss only if asked straight about driving. When told he must not drive: "Not drive at all? That's my living." Becomes more accepting when told treatment usually works and he can get back on the road: "So it's not forever." Asks for a note for work. If given a snoring spray, accept happily (the trap).

ice.ideas: "It's just snoring — my wife exaggerates. Everyone's tired."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terrified of losing his HGV licence and income, so he has been playing down the sleepiness and the near-miss.
ice.expectations: "A spray or strips for the snoring."

cues: "She reckons I stop breathing." — witnessed apnoeas.
"A bit knackered in the day." — invites the Epworth questions.
"Am I going to lose my licence?" — the fear behind the minimising.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA picture (snoring + witnessed apnoeas/gasping + excessive daytime sleepiness + obesity) rather than treating it as simple snoring

Assesses properly — quantifies daytime sleepiness with the EPWORTH scale and considers STOP-Bang (not using Epworth alone to decide referral, NICE NG202), documents witnessed apnoeas, neck circumference/BMI, and screens associated conditions (hypertension, AF, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risk)
Asks DIRECTLY about sleepiness while DRIVING and near-misses/accidents (he has volunteered a near-miss at the wheel)

Refers for a SLEEP STUDY/sleep-service assessment to confirm and grade OSA, flagged for rapid assessment as a vocational driver (NICE NG202), and advises lifestyle measures (weight loss, avoid alcohol/sedatives, side-sleeping, smoking) and that CPAP is highly effective for moderate-severe OSA (and considered for mild OSA with symptoms affecting daily life)

Addresses the DVLA DUTY clearly: advises NOT to drive while sleepy, explains the LEGAL obligation to notify the DVLA if the sleepiness is not controlled within 3 months or once moderate/severe OSA with sleepiness is confirmed (same medical standard for GROUP 2/HGV, with at least annual licence review), that it is the patient’s responsibility, and documents the advice
Recognises the minimisation driven by fear for his livelihood, takes the snoring complaint seriously while conveying the genuine danger, and does NOT collude with "just give me a spray"
Handles the driving/DVLA conversation honestly but supportively — explaining that effective treatment usually allows a return to driving — and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: sleep-study referral and timeline, the driving advice documented (and GMC route if he continues to drive against advice), lifestyle plan, comorbidity review, and follow-up — OSA assessment + DVLA duty, not a snoring remedy and a wave-off

worked.txt: "I’ll absolutely help with the snoring — but what your wife describes, the stopping and gasping, plus you being shattered and nearly nodding off driving, points to something we need to take seriously: a condition called sleep apnoea, where the airway collapses in sleep. That’s more than snoring."

"Let me ask how sleepy you really are — I’ll use a quick scoring scale: how likely are you to doze watching TV, sitting reading, in a meeting, stopped in traffic? … And your collar size — and I’d like your blood pressure checked at the surgery, as I can’t measure it over video and apnoea often pushes it up. There’s a second short questionnaire too, because the sleepiness score alone doesn’t decide things."

"I’m going to refer you for a sleep study to confirm it, and I’ll mark it as a priority because you drive for a living. The good news: it’s very treatable. Losing some weight and cutting alcohol in the evening help a lot, and a machine called CPAP — a mask at night — is brilliant for this; most people feel like a new person and the daytime sleepiness goes."

"Now I have to be straight about driving, because it matters most. You’ve nearly nodded off at the wheel — you must NOT drive while you feel sleepy. And the DVLA rules apply: you mustn’t drive while you’re sleepy, and if it isn’t under control within 3 months, or the study confirms moderate or severe apnoea, you have a legal duty to tell them. The rules are the same for your HGV licence, but it’s reviewed at least every year."

"I know that’s frightening with your job — but here’s the important part: once it’s treated and the sleepiness is controlled, people usually get back to driving, including professionally. Sorting this protects your licence long-term, and protects you and others now."

"I’ll write down that I’ve advised you not to drive while sleepy and when you must notify the DVLA. Please don’t drive to the sleep study sleepy — get a lift. If anything changes I’m here, and we’ll review once the study and treatment are sorted."

f.learning: Snoring with WITNESSED APNOEAS (partner-observed pauses/gasping), excessive daytime SLEEPINESS and obesity is the classic picture of OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA — not simple snoring — with supporting features of unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, nocturia, poor concentration, reduced libido and a large neck circumference. Assess properly: quantify daytime sleepiness with the EPWORTH Sleepiness Scale and consider STOP-Bang (NICE NG202, 2021: the Epworth score alone should not decide referral, because not everyone with OSA is sleepy), document witnessed apnoeas, neck circumference and BMI, and screen the associated/consequent conditions (often resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risk) — and ask DIRECTLY about sleepiness while DRIVING and any near-misses. Refer to a SLEEP SERVICE for a diagnostic SLEEP STUDY to confirm and grade OSA — prioritised for rapid assessment in vocational drivers and safety-critical workers (NICE NG202) — advise lifestyle measures (WEIGHT LOSS often substantially improves or resolves it, avoid ALCOHOL and SEDATIVES, side-sleeping, smoking cessation), and explain that CPAP is highly effective for moderate-severe OSA and transforms daytime sleepiness (NICE NG202 also advises considering CPAP for mild OSA with symptoms affecting daily life; mandibular advancement splints are an option for mild OSA or if CPAP is declined or not tolerated). The critical, examinable point is the DVLA/DRIVING duty: advise the patient NOT to drive while sleepy, explain the LEGAL obligation to notify the DVLA where the condition affects driving — DVLA: with suspected OSA and excessive sleepiness, no driving until the sleepiness is controlled, notification if not controlled within 3 months, and notification of confirmed moderate or severe OSA with excessive sleepiness; the medical criteria are the same for GROUP 2 (HGV/bus) drivers, whose licences are then reviewed at least annually — that it is the patient’s responsibility to notify, document the advice, and (per GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive, 2017) be prepared to inform the DVLA promptly if a patient continues to drive against advice and cannot be dissuaded, telling the patient first where possible. This conversation cannot be skipped because the patient’s livelihood is at stake — handle it honestly but supportively (effective treatment usually allows return to driving), recognising the minimisation driven by fear of losing the licence, and do not collude with "just give me something for the snoring".

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG202 (obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s, 2021) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (respiratory and sleep conditions) · [3] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) · [4] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults, 2019, updated 2026) · [5] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults) · [6] NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation, 2021)
knowledge.summary: Snoring with witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness, obesity and a near-miss at the wheel is suspected OSA, not simple snoring. Assess with the Epworth score and STOP-Bang, refer for rapid sleep assessment because he is a vocational driver, and tell him clearly that he must not drive while sleepy. Explain the DVLA rules honestly and supportively, and document the advice.

points.t: Loud snoring, witnessed pauses and gasping, unrefreshing sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness, with obesity and a large neck, is the typical picture of OSAHS. Other clues: morning headache, nocturia, poor concentration, irritability, low libido.

NICE NG202 [1]: use the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and consider STOP-Bang, but do not use the Epworth score alone to decide on referral, because not everyone with OSAHS is sleepy. Record BMI, neck circumference, blood pressure, and ask about alcohol, sedatives and smoking.

NICE NG202 [1]: prioritise rapid sleep-service assessment for people with suspected OSAHS who drive vocationally, work in safety-critical roles, have unstable cardiovascular disease, or are pregnant. A lorry driver with a near-miss meets this.

NICE NG202 [1]: lifestyle advice for everyone (weight loss, alcohol reduction, stopping smoking, sleep position). Fixed-level CPAP for moderate or severe OSAHS; consider CPAP for mild OSAHS with symptoms affecting daily life; a customised mandibular advancement splint is an option for mild OSAHS or if CPAP is declined or not tolerated. Severity by AHI: mild below 15, moderate 15 to 29, severe 30 or more.

DVLA [2]: “excessive sleepiness” means sleepiness having, or likely to have, an adverse effect on driving. With suspected OSAS and excessive sleepiness he must not drive until the sleepiness is satisfactorily controlled; DVLA must be told if control is not achieved within 3 months. Moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepiness must be notified. Once controlled and adherent on treatment, drivers are usually relicensed; Group 2 licences are then reviewed at least annually. It is the driver’s legal duty to notify.

GMC (2017) [3]: explain the condition’s effect on driving and the duty to notify, and document it. If a patient continues to drive when not safe and cannot be persuaded to stop, the GP should contact the DVLA promptly, telling the patient first where possible.
Check blood pressure (OSA is linked with resistant hypertension, NICE NG136 [4]), HbA1c (NICE NG28 [5]), pulse rhythm for atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196 [6]) and cardiovascular risk.

model.text: Hello Mr Malhotra, I’m Dr Clarke. What can I do for you today?

Doc, my wife’s threatening to sleep in the spare room — my snoring’s that bad. She reckons I stop breathing and gasp, but she exaggerates. I’m a bit knackered in the day, sure, but who isn’t? Can you just give me a spray or strips or something?

I’ll definitely help with the snoring. What your wife describes, plus being tired, makes me want to understand the whole picture first, so whatever we do actually works. Can I ask some questions and then we’ll plan?
model.why: Takes the request seriously and agrees an agenda

model.text: Fair enough.
Tell me more about what your wife sees at night.
She says I go quiet, then gasp and snort like I’m choking. She’s been nudging me.
And in the day — how likely are you to doze off watching TV, sitting reading, as a passenger, or sitting in traffic? I’ll give each a score out of three — it’s called the Epworth scale.
model.why: Quantifies sleepiness with the Epworth scale

model.text: TV, definitely. Reading, yes. Traffic… sometimes.
You mentioned traffic. You drive a lorry for work, don’t you? Have you ever felt yourself nodding off at the wheel, or had any near-misses?
model.why: Asks directly about sleepiness while driving

model.text: (pause) Once, recently. I caught myself drifting. Scared me, to be honest.
Thank you for telling me — I know that wasn’t easy. Do you wake unrefreshed, with headaches in the morning, or get up to pass water at night?
I wake up feeling like I haven’t slept.
How much alcohol do you drink, especially in the evening? Any sleeping tablets or other medicines? And do you smoke?
A drink in the evening now and then. No tablets.
Has anyone ever told you your blood pressure or sugar is high, or that your heart beats irregularly? And what’s your collar size?
Not that I know. Collar size — I’d have to check.
When you think about all this, what’s worrying you most?
Honestly? The job. If this is something, am I going to lose my licence? I’ve got bills.
That’s a completely understandable worry, and I’m glad you’ve said it. I’ll be straight with you about driving, and I’ll also tell you the good news.

What you’re describing — heavy snoring, stopping breathing and gasping, feeling unrefreshed and dozing in the day — sounds like obstructive sleep apnoea. The airway at the back of the throat collapses during sleep, your oxygen dips, and your brain wakes you briefly many times a night without you knowing. That’s why you’re so tired.
model.why: Names suspected OSA and explains it

model.text: So it’s not just snoring.

It’s more than snoring. A spray or strips won’t fix it. I’m going to refer you to the sleep clinic for a sleep study, and because you drive for a living I’ll mark it as a priority. It’s very treatable. Losing some weight and cutting evening alcohol help, and many people use a mask at night called CPAP. Most feel like a new person.
model.why: Priority sleep referral (NG202), lifestyle and CPAP

model.text: Right. And the lorry?

This is the important part. Because you’re sleepy and you’ve drifted at the wheel, you must not drive — lorry or car — until the sleepiness is under control. That’s for your safety and everyone else’s on the road.
Not drive at all? That’s my living.

I know, and I’m sorry — that’s hard to hear. Here’s the good news: once sleep apnoea is treated and the sleepiness is controlled, most people get back to driving, professional drivers included. The DVLA rules are: while this is being looked into, you don’t drive. If it isn’t controlled within three months, or the study shows moderate or severe apnoea, you must tell the DVLA yourself. For your lorry licence, they’ll then want the sleep clinic to confirm it’s controlled, and review it every year.
model.why: Explains DVLA rules accurately and supportively

model.text: So it’s not forever.

For most people, no. Getting treated quickly is the fastest way back to work. Would it help to talk about what you’ll say to work? That’s your conversation to have — I won’t contact them without your agreement, but I can do a fit note if you can’t do your usual job.
Yeah, a note would help.
I’d also like you to come in so the nurse can check your blood pressure, weight and neck size, a pulse check, and a blood test for sugar — sleep apnoea often goes with those.
Please don’t drive to the sleep clinic — get a lift. I’m writing down today that I’ve advised you not to drive and explained the DVLA rules. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do?
No driving till it’s sorted. Sleep study. Tell the DVLA if it’s moderate or worse, or not sorted in three months. Cut back the evening drink. Come in for the checks.

Exactly right. I’ll see you after the sleep study. If you notice chest pain, a racing irregular heartbeat or feel really unwell, get seen urgently. And if you ever feel you can’t manage without driving, talk to me first — we’ll work it out together.
model.why: Follow-up, safety-net and an open door on driving

social.t: Loss of income drives minimisation. Offer a fit note and practical help; a quick referral is the fastest route back to work.
His wife’s observations are key evidence and her sleep is affected too. Treating OSA usually helps both.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: with excessive sleepiness from suspected OSAS he must not drive until controlled, and must notify if not controlled within 3 months; moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepiness must be notified. Group 2 relicensing requires confirmed control and adherence with at least annual review.
GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive (2017): advise, document, try to persuade; if he continues to drive unsafely, inform the DVLA promptly, telling him first where possible.
A fit note can state he is not fit for driving duties but may be fit for other work with adjustments.

professional.t: The GP’s duty to other road users can outweigh confidentiality when a patient keeps driving unsafely. Handle it transparently and supportively.
Record the Epworth score, the near-miss, the advice not to drive, the DVLA explanation and the patient’s response.

community.t: The Sleep Apnoea Trust and Hope2Sleep for patient information; local weight management services; employer occupational health if he chooses to involve them.

redFlags: Near-miss or sleepiness at the wheel
Very high Epworth score or falling asleep in active situations
Resistant hypertension, AF or heart failure
psychosocial: Fear of losing his HGV licence and income
His wife’s sleep and relationship strain
ice: Idea: “It’s just bad snoring — my wife exaggerates.”

playbook.diagnosis: “This sounds like obstructive sleep apnoea. It explains the snoring, the gasping your wife sees, and why you’re so tired in the day.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “When you’re asleep, the soft tissues at the back of your throat flop closed like a floppy straw. Your oxygen drops, your brain jolts you awake to breathe, and that happens many times a night — so you never get proper rest.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about your job — that’s exactly why getting this treated quickly matters, because treatment is the route back to driving.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a fit note; respect his choice about telling his employer; be clear that the DVLA duty is his and that you will help.
sharedPlan: Priority sleep-service referral as a vocational driver (NICE NG202); Epworth and STOP-Bang recorded
Weight loss, less evening alcohol, no sedatives; CPAP if confirmed
BP, BMI, neck size, pulse rhythm, HbA1c
safetyNet: Must not drive while sleepy; DVLA notification if moderate or severe, or not controlled within 3 months
Advice documented; GMC route if he continues to drive unsafely

pitfalls.intro: This station is designed to test whether you raise driving with a man whose income depends on it. Most candidates recognise OSA; fewer ask about the wheel directly and give accurate, kind DVLA advice.

items.fail: Offering a snoring spray or mouth strips.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Witnessed apnoeas and sleepiness need a sleep study (NICE NG202).
items.fix: Name suspected sleep apnoea and refer.

items.fail: Never asking about sleepiness while driving.
items.why: The near-miss is the central safety issue; missing it misses the station.
items.fix: “You drive for work — have you ever felt yourself nodding off at the wheel?”

items.fail: Telling him he must notify the DVLA today, or that he will lose his licence permanently.
items.why: Inaccurate advice. DVLA: stop driving while sleepy; notify if moderate or severe OSAS is confirmed, or if not controlled within 3 months; relicensing follows control.
items.fix: Give the rule accurately and the route back to driving.

items.fail: Avoiding the driving advice because he is worried about his job.
items.why: Collusion on public safety is a serious professional failing (GMC 2017).
items.fix: Name the worry, then be clear: “You mustn’t drive while sleepy — and here’s how we get you back.”

items.fail: Routine referral with no priority for a vocational driver.
items.why: NICE NG202 prioritises rapid assessment for vocational drivers.
items.fix: Mark the referral as a priority and say why.

items.fail: Driving advice given but not documented.
items.why: Documentation protects the patient, the public and the GP; it is expected feedback.
items.fix: Say it and write it: “I’m recording that I’ve advised you not to drive.”

Fear for his licence and income. Name it.
Suspected OSA; priority sleep referral; CPAP and lifestyle; must not drive while sleepy.
DVLA rules with the route back to driving; fit note; checks; documentation; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Offers a snoring spray; never asks about driving; or asks, but then avoids the driving advice because of his job; no referral or documentation.
wordPics.pass: Recognises OSA, uses the Epworth score, refers to the sleep service, advises him not to drive while sleepy and explains the DVLA duty.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks directly about near-misses and responds to the disclosure warmly; prioritises the referral as a vocational driver (NICE NG202); explains the DVLA rules accurately with the route back to work; offers a fit note; documents the advice; checks BP, HbA1c and rhythm.

avoid.dont: “Try a nasal spray and sleeping on your side.”
avoid.instead: “What your wife describes sounds like more than snoring — I want to check for sleep apnoea.”
avoid.why: Treating OSA as simple snoring misses a dangerous, treatable condition.

avoid.instead: “You mustn’t drive while you’re sleepy — and once it’s treated, most people get back to driving.”
avoid.why: Accurate and hopeful advice keeps him engaged and honest.

avoid.dont: “I have to report you to the DVLA.”
avoid.instead: “It’s your legal duty to tell them if it’s moderate or severe, or not controlled in three months — I’ll help you through it.”
avoid.why: The duty is his; the GP reports only if he keeps driving unsafely against advice (GMC 2017).

The DVLA rules are: while this is being looked into, you don’t drive. If it isn’t controlled within three months, or the study shows moderate or severe apnoea, you must tell the DVLA yourself. For your lorry licence, they’ll then want the sleep clinic to confirm it’s controlled, and review it every year.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains DVLA rules accurately and supportively

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not forever.

For most people, no. Getting treated quickly is the fastest way back to work. Would it help to talk about what you’ll say to work? That’s your conversation to have — I won’t contact them without your agreement, but I can do a fit note if you can’t do your usual job.
Yeah, a note would help.
I’d also like you to come in so the nurse can check your blood pressure, weight and neck size, a pulse check, and a blood test for sugar — sleep apnoea often goes with those.
Please don’t drive to the sleep clinic — get a lift. I’m writing down today that I’ve advised you not to drive and explained the DVLA rules. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do?
No driving till it’s sorted. Sleep study. Tell the DVLA if it’s moderate or worse, or not sorted in three months. Cut back the evening drink. Come in for the checks.

Exactly right. I’ll see you after the sleep study. If you notice chest pain, a racing irregular heartbeat or feel really unwell, get seen urgently. And if you ever feel you can’t manage without driving, talk to me first — we’ll work it out together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Follow-up, safety-net and an open door on driving

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG202 (obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s, 2021) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (respiratory and sleep conditions) · [3] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) · [4] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults, 2019, updated 2026) · [5] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults) · [6] NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation, 2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Snoring with witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness, obesity and a near-miss at the wheel is suspected OSA, not simple snoring. Assess with the Epworth score and STOP-Bang, refer for rapid sleep assessment because he is a vocational driver, and tell him clearly that he must not drive while sleepy. Explain the DVLA rules honestly and supportively, and document the advice.

points.t: Loud snoring, witnessed pauses and gasping, unrefreshing sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness, with obesity and a large neck, is the typical picture of OSAHS. Other clues: morning headache, nocturia, poor concentration, irritability, low libido.

NICE NG202 [1]: use the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and consider STOP-Bang, but do not use the Epworth score alone to decide on referral, because not everyone with OSAHS is sleepy. Record BMI, neck circumference, blood pressure, and ask about alcohol, sedatives and smoking.

NICE NG202 [1]: prioritise rapid sleep-service assessment for people with suspected OSAHS who drive vocationally, work in safety-critical roles, have unstable cardiovascular disease, or are pregnant. A lorry driver with a near-miss meets this.

NICE NG202 [1]: lifestyle advice for everyone (weight loss, alcohol reduction, stopping smoking, sleep position). Fixed-level CPAP for moderate or severe OSAHS; consider CPAP for mild OSAHS with symptoms affecting daily life; a customised mandibular advancement splint is an option for mild OSAHS or if CPAP is declined or not tolerated. Severity by AHI: mild below 15, moderate 15 to 29, severe 30 or more.

DVLA [2]: “excessive sleepiness” means sleepiness having, or likely to have, an adverse effect on driving. With suspected OSAS and excessive sleepiness he must not drive until the sleepiness is satisfactorily controlled; DVLA must be told if control is not achieved within 3 months. Moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepiness must be notified. Once controlled and adherent on treatment, drivers are usually relicensed; Group 2 licences are then reviewed at least annually. It is the driver’s legal duty to notify.

GMC (2017) [3]: explain the condition’s effect on driving and the duty to notify, and document it. If a patient continues to drive when not safe and cannot be persuaded to stop, the GP should contact the DVLA promptly, telling the patient first where possible.
Check blood pressure (OSA is linked with resistant hypertension, NICE NG136 [4]), HbA1c (NICE NG28 [5]), pulse rhythm for atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196 [6]) and cardiovascular risk.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged the snoring request before widening the question.
Occupation and livelihood, evening alcohol, sedatives, smoking and wife’s concerns.
Picked up “who isn’t tired” and the near-miss in traffic, and explored both.
Idea (just snoring), concern (losing his licence and income), expectation (a spray or strips).
Epworth score with STOP-Bang (NICE NG202); BP, BMI, neck circumference, pulse rhythm, HbA1c.
OSA versus simple snoring; contributors (weight, alcohol); other causes of sleepiness.
Asked directly about sleepiness at the wheel and near-misses; screened cardiovascular associations.
Named suspected obstructive sleep apnoea and explained the mechanism.
Priority sleep-service referral as a vocational driver; lifestyle; CPAP explained; not to drive while sleepy.
Hypertension, diabetes and AF checks; fit note for work; confidentiality respected.
DVLA rules explained and documented; teach-back; follow-up after the study; GMC route held in reserve.

social.t: Loss of income drives minimisation. Offer a fit note and practical help; a quick referral is the fastest route back to work.
His wife’s observations are key evidence and her sleep is affected too. Treating OSA usually helps both.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: with excessive sleepiness from suspected OSAS he must not drive until controlled, and must notify if not controlled within 3 months; moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepiness must be notified. Group 2 relicensing requires confirmed control and adherence with at least annual review.
GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive (2017): advise, document, try to persuade; if he continues to drive unsafely, inform the DVLA promptly, telling him first where possible.
A fit note can state he is not fit for driving duties but may be fit for other work with adjustments.

professional.t: The GP’s duty to other road users can outweigh confidentiality when a patient keeps driving unsafely. Handle it transparently and supportively.
Record the Epworth score, the near-miss, the advice not to drive, the DVLA explanation and the patient’s response.

community.t: The Sleep Apnoea Trust and Hope2Sleep for patient information; local weight management services; employer occupational health if he chooses to involve them.

redFlags: Near-miss or sleepiness at the wheel
Very high Epworth score or falling asleep in active situations
Resistant hypertension, AF or heart failure

His wife’s sleep and relationship strain
ice: Idea: “It’s just bad snoring — my wife exaggerates.”
Concern: losing his licence and his job

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like obstructive sleep apnoea. It explains the snoring, the gasping your wife sees, and why you’re so tired in the day.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “When you’re asleep, the soft tissues at the back of your throat flop closed like a floppy straw. Your oxygen drops, your brain jolts you awake to breathe, and that happens many times a night — so you never get proper rest.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about your job — that’s exactly why getting this treated quickly matters, because treatment is the route back to driving.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a fit note; respect his choice about telling his employer; be clear that the DVLA duty is his and that you will help.
sharedPlan: Priority sleep-service referral as a vocational driver (NICE NG202); Epworth and STOP-Bang recorded
Weight loss, less evening alcohol, no sedatives; CPAP if confirmed
BP, BMI, neck size, pulse rhythm, HbA1c
safetyNet: Must not drive while sleepy; DVLA notification if moderate or severe, or not controlled within 3 months
Advice documented; GMC route if he continues to drive unsafely

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is designed to test whether you raise driving with a man whose income depends on it. Most candidates recognise OSA; fewer ask about the wheel directly and give accurate, kind DVLA advice.

items.fail: Offering a snoring spray or mouth strips.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Witnessed apnoeas and sleepiness need a sleep study (NICE NG202).
items.fix: Name suspected sleep apnoea and refer.

items.fail: Never asking about sleepiness while driving.
items.why: The near-miss is the central safety issue; missing it misses the station.
items.fix: “You drive for work — have you ever felt yourself nodding off at the wheel?”

items.fail: Telling him he must notify the DVLA today, or that he will lose his licence permanently.
items.why: Inaccurate advice. DVLA: stop driving while sleepy; notify if moderate or severe OSAS is confirmed, or if not controlled within 3 months; relicensing follows control.
items.fix: Give the rule accurately and the route back to driving.

items.fail: Avoiding the driving advice because he is worried about his job.
items.why: Collusion on public safety is a serious professional failing (GMC 2017).
items.fix: Name the worry, then be clear: “You mustn’t drive while sleepy — and here’s how we get you back.”

items.fail: Routine referral with no priority for a vocational driver.
items.why: NICE NG202 prioritises rapid assessment for vocational drivers.
items.fix: Mark the referral as a priority and say why.

items.fail: Driving advice given but not documented.
items.why: Documentation protects the patient, the public and the GP; it is expected feedback.
items.fix: Say it and write it: “I’m recording that I’ve advised you not to drive.”
